aspect: There is no right answer to copy
description: Different professional translators make different legitimate transliteration choices. Maryam on a mother's passport and Mariam on her child's birth certificate triggers questions about whether the documents establish the family relationship at all.
energy_note: Your daughter's birth certificate doesn't match you.

aspect: Systems that match exact text generate false discrepancies
description: Where records hold different transliterations, exact-match systems produce mismatches that delay onboarding, increase manual review and flag legitimate customers - across passports, licences, applications, credit bureaus and watchlists.

Arabic naming convention is first name, father's name, grandfather's name, family name. Systems built for that force two-part names into four fields by splitting or duplicating; systems built for two reject four. Either way the output differs from the input.
energy_note: A name that doesn't fit the boxes in either direction.

description: Inconsistent names create E-Verify failures, background check mismatches and banking or credit issues that persist long after any immigration status is resolved.
energy_note: A typo from 2009, still failing checks in 2026.

aspect: And correcting it is slow and charged for
description: Correcting a green card error requires Form I-90, cited at $455 and 6-12 months to process - for a mistake made by the agency that issued it.
energy_note: Four hundred dollars and a year, for their typo.

description: A mother's passport spelled Maryam and her child's birth certificate spelled Mariam triggers questions about whether the documents establish the family relationship at all. Both spellings are legitimate transliterations; there is no correct one to have used.
energy_note: One letter between you and proving she is your daughter.
